newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican Zapatista women demand peace.
newsitem.headline: Mexican Zapatista women demand peace.

text.p: Thousands of peasant Mayan women celebrated Women's Day on Saturday by taking to the streets to demand the Mexican government restart stalled peace talks with Zapatista guerrillas in the southern state of Chiapas.

Wearing ski-masks that have become a trademark of the rebel Zapatista Army for National Liberation (EZLN), some 5,000 Tzeltal and Tzotzil Indian women marched and chanted anti-government slogans in this remote hamlet some 350 miles (560 km) southeast of Mexico City.

Shouting "Long live the EZLN" and "Long live Marcos," the rebel movement's charismatic leader, the women demanded Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo get peace talks back on track after they derailed late last year.
Dressed in brightly coloured Mayan clothing, the women urged Zedillo abide by an agreement on Indian rights reached between the rebels and a legislative commission early last year.

The government made changes to the agreement late last year, saying it violated Mexico's constitution by granting too much autonomy to Indians. The move sparked an angry response from the rebels, who broke off talks that had been held so far in this mountainous village.
"Zedillo has said he wants to solve the conflict. Then he should accept the initiative on Indian rights," read a document signed by the women.
Many of the women had walked for hours from nearby communities to attend the march. Many were also barefoot, wearing only black woollen skirts and rainbow coloured tops.
Some of the women shouted at nearby soldiers, who in the three years since the rebellion began have build a garrison on top of a hill that overlooks the village.
"Out of our town, you murderers," one woman shouted.
Another woman hoisted a poster that read "Zedillo: women do not give up and are not for sale."

Rebel leader Marcos, a mixture of Indian and Spanish like most Mexicans, accused the Mexican army on Friday of using the break in the talks to strengthen their positions in the area, but he denied press reports that the rebels were completely surrounded.

The Zapatistas launched a surprise rebellion on Jan. 1, 1994, fighting the Mexican army for two weeks before peace talks began. At least 150 people died in the first days of the uprising for greater democracy and Indian rights.
Chiapas is considered Mexico's most backward state, where landowners often take the law into their own hands to evict peasant farmers that squat on their holdings.
